prediction.whatIsNeededForEstimate: The appraisal report's stated value of the property with the concrete batch plant as its highest and best use (pre-rezoning), the appraised or estimated value of the property under the post-rezoning restrictions (its value for permitted light-industrial uses other than a batch plant), and any dollar figure from Maib's own trial testimony as to the property's value or the amount of loss he is claiming. Also useful: the specific compensation amount (if any) demanded in the operative Bert Harris Act notice of claim or complaint, and documentation of the costs Maib incurred in site preparation (wells, clearing, tree relocation) if those are being separately claimed.
prediction.likelyOutcome: Liability under the Bert Harris Act is conceded by prior appellate ruling, and Maib enters the damages trial with a substantial tactical advantage after excluding the County's two valuation experts and securing the right to testify to his own property's value. He is very likely to recover a meaningful compensation award reflecting the loss in value from losing the concrete batch plant use, but the record provided contains no appraisal figure, before/after valuation, or stated damages demand from which to compute an actual dollar range.

issues.label: Bert Harris Act compensation for loss of concrete batch plant use
Exclusion of County's valuation and economic-feasibility experts
Admissibility of owner's own opinion testimony on property value
Risk of partial-loss or substitute-use offset argument by County

outcome.description: At a four-day jury trial in September 2019, with the County's economist and appraiser excluded, the jury awarded the landowner $2 million; final judgment was entered for $2 million plus $1,302,577 in prejudgment interest. The Fourth District affirmed on November 25, 2020. Amount used excludes prejudgment interest.
